newsitem.title: UK: Refugee aid airlift needs ceasefire, airport data.
newsitem.headline: Refugee aid airlift needs ceasefire, airport data.

text.p: Civilian airlift companies said the lack of both a ceasefire and firm information on the state of local airports, especially at Goma, are holding up the chartering of cargo aircraft to airlift relief supplies to tackle the Zairean refugee crisis.
"Everyone is waiting for a cease-fire. We've had lots of requests for flights to Zaire, and it will get very busy once the situation improves," said one air cargo charter broker.

"We have had enquiries from a number of air cargo charter brokers, who have been approached by various governments and aid organisations," said Vince Seeger, sales manager for HeavyLift Cargo Airlines, based at Stansted.
HeavyLift operates a range of freighter aircraft including the world's largest, the Russian Antonov An-124 freighter able to carry a maximum of 150 tonnes.
Cost is a key factor in the enquiries on aircraft availability, Seeger added but,"we need more information before we can provide costs."

"We need to know what our exact mission will be, what sort of cargo we will be carrying and to where. What are the runway conditions, ground handling and security conditions and possible access to fuel supplies also need to be taken into account," he said.
A United Nations High Commission for Refugees(UNHCR) spokesman told Reuters from Geneva that an assessment team had left Kinshasa for eastern Zaire on Wednesday morning.
"They'll take two days to get there and will link up with a World Food Programme team. They will be looking at supply routes including airport conditions," he added.
One London air broker said he understood there were substantial aid supplies building up in Nairobi but these could not be moved by air until there was a ceasefire.
It is unlikely that anyone would risk their crew and aircraft until the situation is clearer on the ground, he added.

The Bordeaux-based logistics manager Medicins Sans Frontieres(MSF) Alain Grall told Reuters that they would be able to move quickly once "there was clearer knowledge of local conditions and security."
"Once we've got some assurances, we should be able to reach the area in 24 hours using Boeing 707 or DC-8 aircraft, carrying around 35 tonnes," he added.
An air broker said that a number of these aircraft are alreday based in Africa and will be cheaper to operate than those from elsewhere. They may play a key role in the first part of any airlift.
"Very preliminary enquiries" have been made by Britain's Overseas Development Assistance department about the cost of moving supplies and equipment to the region, an ODA spokesman said.
Antonov-124 aircraft are also operated by another British cargo charter company, Air Foyle Ltd based at Luton.
The carrier's project director, Bruce Bird said they were checking to make sure a positive response could be given if aircraft were requested.
"We are ensuring a complete summary of our capability at any time so that if we should be asked, we should be able to make a positive response."

An executive from leading air charter broker, Chapman Freeborn Marketing Ltd, declined to comment on market suggestions that the company was actively seeking aircraft for several European governments as well as aid organisations.
"I'm not in a position to talk about that. It is a matter between us and our clients," he said. --Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax +44 171 542 5017
